Several publicly available test feeders were considered for the selection of an appropriate feeder for this study. Table 1 shows the different test feeders considered. Among these feeders, EPRI J1 feeder was selected as per the project team’s discussion. The J1 feeder contains a greater number of voltage regulators and capacitors. In this project, we studied the application of medium voltage solid-state transformers, its value and impact in coordination with the voltage regulators, so the EPRI J1 feeder best suited the selection criteria. Figure 1 shows the J1 feeder topology. This feeder is in the northeastern US and consists of around 1300 customers including residential, commercial, and light industrial customers. It has 58 circuit miles of primary network. Almost 30% of PV penetration exists in this feeder model. Table 1. Figure 1. EPRI J1 feeder topology. Solid state transformer model: A solid-state transformer is a power electronic transformer, an AC-to-AC converter. It enables bi-directional power flow and can enhance power quality performance. It can support different smart grid challenges over conventional transformers such as voltage sag compensation, instantaneous voltage regulation, harmonic compensation, power factor correction, auto- balancing, short circuit protection, and variable-frequency output [1]. The SST model in OpenDSS is represented as two different components. A medium voltage load on the MV (primary) side and a low voltage source on the LV (secondary) side as shown in Figure 2. The LV side supplies the power required by the loads on the LV side and maintains a constant voltage at the secondary terminal. As SST supports bidirectional power flow, this SST model can operate in 2 modes: Load mode and Generator mode. The load on the MV side resembles the SST behavior. The active power on the MV load is equal to the active power supplied by the LV source plus the SST losses. It equals the active power injected from the LV terminal minus the SST losses, in case of reverse power flow.
